docs.text: HardFOC core library HardFOC Core ¶ The layer between the HardFOC device drivers and a board HAL. hf-core wraps each driver in a thread-safe handler that takes Base* interfaces, collects the MCU interfaces, RTOS wrappers and utilities, and builds and tests all of it on a host machine with no MCU toolchain. Quickstart Handlers Source on GitHub A device driver knows its chip and nothing else: it talks through a small CRTP interface and leaves locking, bring-up order and bus sharing to its user. A board HAL knows its pins and buses. hf-core is what sits between them, so that every HAL wires a TMC9660 or a BNO08x the same way and no code above the HAL includes an MCU SDK. Where hf-core sits Figure description and sources From the bottom up. Each device driver is its own repository and talks to its chip through a small CRTP interface; hf-core-drivers collects them as submodules, together with hf-internal-interface-wrap (the Base* interfaces and their ESP32 and STM32 implementations) and hf-pincfg. hf-core-utils collects the RTOS wrapper, the general utilities and the CANopen helpers. hf-core's handlers sit on top of those three: each one wraps one driver behind a thread-safe API that takes Base* interfaces. A board HAL creates the MCU peripherals, constructs the handlers it needs and exposes managers; a product is firmware on one board HAL. The driver list is read from cmake/hf_core_build_settings.cmake and the handler list from handlers/. Drawn from: cmake/hf_core_build_settings.cmake driver and utility paths ; handlers/ handler folders ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/platform-layers.py . What you get ¶ 23 handlers, one per device family. Each takes BaseSpi , BaseI2c , BaseUart , BaseGpio or BaseAdc references, initialises its driver on first use and serialises calls with a recursive mutex. See Handlers . One CMake file for every consumer. cmake/hf_core_build_settings.cmake turns HF_CORE_ENABLE_* switches into sources, include directories, ESP-IDF requirements and compile definitions. See Integration and Feature switches . A host build with mocks. HF_CORE_MCU=NONE , HF_CORE_RTOS=NONE : handlers, drivers and utilities compile and run on Linux or macOS against scriptable fakes of the Base* interfaces. See Host build and mocks . Threads and locking without the RTOS in your code. RtosMutex , MutexLockGuard , BaseThread and the OS abstraction map to FreeRTOS on target and to a no-op backend with a fake clock on the host. See Threading and RTOS . CANopen helpers on BaseCan . Frame builders and parsers for NMT, SDO, heartbeat, emergency and CiA 402, and a bridge to any BaseCan . See CANopen . A checked MCU boundary. Only the interface implementations and a short list of files may include vendor headers; the host build proves the rest is portable. See MCU boundary . Used by ¶ Repository Uses hf-core for hf-hal-vortex-v1 Vortex V1: TMC9660, AS5047U, BNO08x, PCAL95555, PCA9685, NTC and WS2812 handlers, the Vortex driver, CANopen hf-hal-flux-v1 Flux V1: ADS7952, MCP9700, NTC, TLE92466ED, MAX22200, Alicat BASIS-2, FDO2 and WS2812 handlers, CANopen hf-utils-and-drivers Superseded by hf-core; kept for older projects Where to go next ¶ Quickstart Add hf-core to a project and drive a handler in 20 lines. Product product firmware repositories Tasks, control loops, protocols No Board HAL hf-hal-vortex-v1 , hf-hal-flux-v1 Creates the buses and pins, constructs the handlers, exposes managers Yes, in its platform files only Handlers hf-core handlers/ One thread-safe class per device family over Base* interfaces No Device drivers hf-core-drivers external/ One repository per chip, CRTP interface, no heap No Interfaces hf-internal-interface-wrap (in hf-core-drivers internal/ ) BaseSpi , BaseI2c , BaseUart , BaseCan , BaseGpio , BaseAdc , ... and their Esp* / Stm* implementations Only the implementations Pin maps hf-pincfg (in hf-core-drivers internal/ ) Functional pin tables per board Board-specific Utilities hf-core-utils : hf-utils-rtos-wrap, hf-utils-general, hf-utils-canopen RTOS wrapper, containers and filters, CANopen frames Only the RTOS backends hf-core pins one commit of hf-core-drivers and one of hf-core-utils as submodules, so a HAL that pins hf-core gets a set of drivers, interfaces and utilities that were built and tested together. One call, through the layers ¶ A HAL manager reads the rotor angle from the AS5047U. Only the last step knows it runs on an ESP32. sequenceDiagram participant M as HAL manager participant H as As5047uHandler participant D as AS5047U driver participant A as As5047uSpiAdapter participant S as BaseSpi (EspSpi on ESP32) M->>H: visitDriver([](auto& d) { return d.GetAngle(); }) H->>H: lock the handler mutex, EnsureInitialized() H->>D: GetAngle() D->>A: transfer(tx, rx, len), static dispatch A->>S: Transfer(tx, rx, len) S-->>D: frame with CRC (retried on a CRC error) D-->>M: 14-bit angle, mutex released Design choices ¶ Choice Why Drivers are CRTP templates, handlers are plain classes The driver dispatch costs nothing; the handler gives HAL code one non-template type per chip Handlers take Base* references and never own them The HAL decides bus sharing and lifetime; a test passes a mock Lazy initialisation Constructing a handler never touches the bus, so construction order does not matter at boot One recursive mutex per handler, optional shared bus mutex Methods may call each other; devices on one bus can share a lock Raw function pointers with void* user_data for low-level callbacks No std::function and no heap on interrupt paths The host build is part of CI It is the proof that everything above the interfaces is free of vendor headers Source map ¶ Path Contents handlers/<chip>/ One handler: its CRTP adapter(s), the handler class, wrappers that expose it as BaseGpio , BaseAdc , BaseTemperature handlers/common/ HandlerCommon.h (delays, log routing), PlatformMutexBackend.h , the CANopen bridge handlers/logger/ The Logger singleton and the per-MCU backend factories cmake/hf_core_build_settings.cmake The build entry point for every consumer CMakeLists.txt , CMakePresets.json The host build tests/host/ Host unit tests, mocks ( mocks/ ) and the test harness ( support/ ) tests/docs/ The code on these pages, compiled and run by the host build examples/esp32/ ESP32 test applications, one per handler or utility hf-core-drivers/ , hf-core-utils/ Submodules Next: Handler model .

docs.text: CANopen ¶ Build and parse CANopen frames with hf-utils-canopen and send them on any BaseCan through hf-core's bridge. The pieces ¶ Piece Where What it does CanOpen::CanFrame hf-utils-canopen CanFrame.h Classic frame: id , dlc , extended , rtr , data[8] Builders CanOpenUtils.h , CanOpenMotorUtils.h BuildNmt() , BuildSdoDownload() (1, 2 or 4 bytes), BuildSdoUpload() , BuildHeartbeat() , and CiA 402 objects: BuildControlWord() , BuildModeOfOperation() , BuildTargetVelocity() , BuildTargetPosition() , BuildTargetTorque() , profile velocity, acceleration and deceleration, status and actual-value requests Parsers CanOpenExtras.h ParseSdoResponse() (expedited: upload data, download ack, abort code), ParseHeartbeat() , ParseEmergency() , DecodeStatusWord() , NextControlWord() Payload codec CanOpenExtras.h FrameCodec interface to encode or authenticate payloads; PassthroughCodec by default Bridge hf-core handlers/common/canopen/ HfUtilsCanFrameToMessage() / HfUtilsMessageToCanFrame() , HfUtilsCanOpenTransport , CanOpenBaseCanLink ( Open , Write , Read , Close ) CANopenNode driver handlers/common/canopen/CO_driver_vortex.c A CANopenNode (CiA 301) target driver that sends and receives through registered hooks hf-utils-canopen has no dependency on BaseCan ; the bridge lives in hf-core so the utilities stay portable. Turn on HF_CORE_ENABLE_UTILS_CANOPEN for the utilities and HF_CORE_ENABLE_CAN as well for the bridge. Write an object with SDO ¶ tests/docs/canopen.cpp #include "CanOpenBaseCanLink.hpp" #include "CanOpenExtras.h" // Set a node's producer heartbeat time (object 0x1017) to 500 ms and wait for the reply. bool SetHeartbeat ( BaseCan & can , uint8_t node_id ) { CanOpenBaseCanLink link ( can ); if ( ! link . Open ()) { return false ; } if ( ! link . Write ( CanOpen :: BuildSdoDownload ( node_id , 0x1017 , 0x00 , 500 , 2 ))) { return false ; } CanOpen :: CanFrame reply {}; for ( int tries = 0 ; tries < 10 ; ++ tries ) { if ( ! link . Read ( reply , 10 )) { continue ; } const auto r = CanOpen :: ParseSdoResponse ( reply ); if ( r . valid && r . nodeId == node_id && r . index == 0x1017 ) { return r . kind == CanOpen :: SdoResponseKind :: DownloadAck ; // AbortTransfer: see r.abort_code } } return false ; } CanOpenBaseCanLink::Write() calls BaseCan::SendMessage() with a 50 ms timeout; Read() calls ReceiveMessage() . The host build runs this function against hf::host::MockCan with an injected acknowledgement ( tests/docs/doc_snippets_test.cpp ). Enable a CiA 402 drive ¶ DecodeStatusWord() maps a status word to a DriveState ; NextControlWord() gives the command that moves one step toward the state you want: tests/docs/canopen.cpp // One step of bringing a CiA 402 drive to Operation enabled, from its status word. CanOpen :: CanFrame NextEnableStep ( uint8_t node_id , uint16_t status_word ) { const auto state = CanOpen :: DecodeStatusWord ( status_word ); const auto cmd = CanOpen :: NextControlWord ( state , CanOpen :: DriveState :: OperationEnabled ); return CanOpen :: BuildControlWord ( node_id , static_cast < uint16_t > ( cmd )); } From DriveState Command toward OperationEnabled Fault FaultReset SwitchOnDisabled Shutdown ReadyToSwitchOn SwitchOn SwitchedOn (and any other) EnableOperation Frame size ¶ CanOpen::CanFrame is classic CAN (8 bytes); hf_can_message_t is FD-sized. The bridge copies at most dlc bytes, bounded by the 8-byte source buffer, sends classic frames ( is_canfd = false ) and zero-fills the rest. Running a CANopen slave ¶ HF_CORE_ENABLE_CANOPENNODE compiles upstream CANopenNode with CO_driver_vortex.c . The application registers its transmit function with hf_co_driver_register_tx() and feeds received standard frames to hf_co_driver_process_rx() ( hf_co_driver_iface.h ). It needs HF_CORE_ENABLE_UTILS_CANOPEN and a CANopenNode checkout at HF_CORE_CANOPENNODE_ROOT ; the driver uses a FreeRTOS critical section, so it builds for ESP-IDF only. For a CiA 402 host client, see the Vortex driver . Next: Utilities .

docs.text: Handler model ¶ What every handler does the same way: construction, initialisation, locking, driver access, errors and callbacks. Life of a handler ¶ stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Constructed: Handler(BaseSpi&, BaseGpio&, ...) Constructed --> Ready: EnsureInitialized() succeeds Constructed --> Constructed: EnsureInitialized() fails (nothing cached, the next call retries) Ready --> Ready: API calls, each under the handler mutex Ready --> Constructed: Deinitialize() / EnsureDeinitialized() Construct with references to Base* interfaces the HAL owns. The constructor stores them; it does not touch the bus and does not create the driver. Initialise on first use. EnsureInitialized() creates the CRTP driver over the handler's adapter, probes the chip and applies the configuration; it returns at once when already done. Most API methods call it themselves, so an explicit call is only needed to learn early that the chip is absent. Use the typed API. Each public method takes the handler's mutex. The interfaces must outlive the handler. Handlers are neither copyable nor movable. Inside a handler ¶ Piece Example (TMC9660) Role CRTP adapter HalSpiTmc9660Comm , HalUartTmc9660Comm Implements the driver's communication interface with BaseSpi / BaseUart / BaseGpio calls Driver tmc9660::TMC9660<HalSpiTmc9660Comm> The chip logic, from the driver repository Handler Tmc9660Handler Owns adapter and driver, locks, initialises, translates errors Wrappers Tmc9660AdcWrapper , Tmc9660TemperatureWrapper , gpio() Present parts of the chip as BaseAdc , BaseTemperature , BaseGpio so other code can use them like MCU peripherals Other wrappers of the same kind: Pca9685Handler::GetPwmAdapter() (a BasePwm ) and CreateGpioPin() on the PCA9685 and PCAL95555 handlers (a BaseGpio per pin). These return std::shared_ptr and allocate once, when created; create them at start-up. Locking ¶ Every handler except the Logger holds an RtosMutex , a recursive mutex: a locked method can call another public method of the same handler. Two tasks can share one handler. Some devices share a bus with others and must not interleave transactions with them: an RS-485 line with several instruments, or several sensors on one I2C bus. The handlers for those take an optional RtosMutex* bus_mutex ; pass the same mutex to every handler on that bus. A null pointer uses a private one. Takes bus_mutex Bus AlicatBasis2Handler , DynamixelHandler , Fdo2Handler UART (shared line) Bmp581Handler , SfmHandler , Se050Handler I2C tests/docs/threading.cpp // Two flow meters on one I2C bus: give both handlers the same mutex so a // read on one never interleaves with a transaction on the other. struct FlowMeters { FlowMeters ( BaseI2c & inlet_dev , BaseI2c & outlet_dev ) : inlet ( inlet_dev , SfmHandlerConfig {}, & bus_mutex ), outlet ( outlet_dev , SfmHandlerConfig {}, & bus_mutex ) {} RtosMutex bus_mutex ; // declared first: constructed before the handlers SfmHandler inlet ; SfmHandler outlet ; }; Reaching the driver ¶ Handlers expose the methods a HAL needs most. For the rest, use the driver itself: Access Locked? Handlers visitDriver(fn) (or withDriver(fn) ) Yes: takes the mutex, ensures initialisation, calls fn(driver) AS5047U, ADS7952, ADS9324, BNO08x, ISF15ACP4, MAX22200, TLE92466ED, TMC5160, TMC9660, WS2812 GetDriver() , GetSensor() , GetDevice() , driverViaSpi() / driverViaUart() No: the caller synchronises Most handlers; see each handler's method table visitDriver() returns what fn returns, or a default-constructed value when the driver is not available. Errors ¶ Handlers return what fits the interface they stand in for: hf_gpio_err_t for GPIO-like handlers, bool for initialisation, the driver's result type ( sfm::DriverResult<T> , se050 status codes) where the driver has a rich one. Check every result. A failed EnsureInitialized() caches nothing, so the next call tries again; that makes a chip that powers up late recover without special code. Callbacks ¶ Low-level callbacks in the Base* interfaces are plain function pointers with a void* user_data , not std::function , so no heap and no capture on interrupt paths. A handler passes a non-capturing lambda and gets itself back from user_data : int_pin . ConfigureInterrupt ( hf_gpio_interrupt_trigger_t :: HF_GPIO_INTERRUPT_TRIGGER_FALLING_EDGE , []( BaseGpio * , hf_gpio_interrupt_trigger_t , void * ctx ) { static_cast < MyHandler *> ( ctx ) -> OnInterrupt (); }, this ); Handlers that react to an interrupt do the bus work later, in task context: Pcal95555Handler sets a flag in the interrupt and reads the chip in DrainPendingInterrupts() . Next: Threading and RTOS .

Handlers visitDriver(fn) (or withDriver(fn) ) Yes: takes the mutex, ensures initialisation, calls fn(driver) AS5047U, ADS7952, ADS9324, BNO08x, ISF15ACP4, MAX22200, TLE92466ED, TMC5160, TMC9660, WS2812 GetDriver() , GetSensor() , GetDevice() , driverViaSpi() / driverViaUart() No: the caller synchronises Most handlers; see each handler's method table visitDriver() returns what fn returns, or a default-constructed value when the driver is not available.
docs.title: Reaching the driver

docs.text: Handlers return what fits the interface they stand in for: hf_gpio_err_t for GPIO-like handlers, bool for initialisation, the driver's result type ( sfm::DriverResult<T> , se050 status codes) where the driver has a rich one. Check every result. A failed EnsureInitialized() caches nothing, so the next call tries again; that makes a chip that powers up late recover without special code.

docs.text: Low-level callbacks in the Base* interfaces are plain function pointers with a void* user_data , not std::function , so no heap and no capture on interrupt paths. A handler passes a non-capturing lambda and gets itself back from user_data : int_pin . ConfigureInterrupt ( hf_gpio_interrupt_trigger_t :: HF_GPIO_INTERRUPT_TRIGGER_FALLING_EDGE , []( BaseGpio * , hf_gpio_interrupt_trigger_t , void * ctx ) { static_cast < MyHandler *> ( ctx ) -> OnInterrupt (); }, this ); Handlers that react to an interrupt do the bus work later, in task context: Pcal95555Handler sets a flag in the interrupt and reads the chip in DrainPendingInterrupts() . docs.text: Host build and mocks ¶ Build and test hf-core on Linux or macOS with no MCU toolchain, and use its mocks from a board HAL's own host tests. hf-core builds and runs its unit tests on a Linux or macOS machine, with no ESP32 or STM32 toolchain. The host build compiles everything above the MCU layer — handlers, external chip drivers, hf-core-utils and the Base* interfaces — with HF_CORE_MCU=NONE and HF_CORE_RTOS=NONE . Tests drive the handlers through scriptable fakes of BaseI2c , BaseSpi , BaseGpio , BaseAdc , BaseCan , BaseNvs , BaseUart and BaseTemperature . On-target builds do not use this path. ESP-IDF projects keep including cmake/hf_core_build_settings.cmake from their component ( examples/esp32/components/hf_core ), and HAL repositories do the same. Build and run ¶ Requirements: CMake 3.22 or newer, Ninja, and a C++20 compiler (GCC 13 and Clang 17 or newer are tested). Clone with submodules: git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/hardfoc/hf-core.git cd hf-core cmake --preset host-debug cmake --build --preset host-debug ctest --preset host-debug Each file under tests/host/ is one executable and one ctest entry; tests/docs/ adds one more. Run a single executable to see each case, or pass part of a case name to run only matching cases: ./build/host-debug/tests/host/test_pcal95555 ./build/host-debug/tests/host/test_pcal95555 CreateGpioPin To build with another compiler, set it at configure time, for example CC=clang CXX=clang++ cmake --preset host-debug . Static analysis ¶ Both tools read build/host-debug/compile_commands.json , so configure first. They analyse hf-core's own sources only ( handlers/ , tests/host/ ; see tools/lint/own_sources.py ) and fail on any finding. bash tools/lint/run-clang-tidy.sh build/host-debug # checks: tools/lint/host.clang-tidy bash tools/lint/run-cppcheck.sh build/host-debug # policy: tools/lint/cppcheck-suppressions.txt CI pins clang-tidy 18 and cppcheck 2.13 (Ubuntu 24.04). With a Homebrew clang-tidy on macOS, point it at the SDK: CLANG_TIDY=$(brew --prefix llvm)/bin/clang-tidy CLANG_TIDY_EXTRA_ARG="-isysroot$(xcrun --show-sdk-path)" . .github/workflows/host.yml runs the build and tests with GCC and Clang, then clang-tidy and cppcheck. Its CI gate job passes only when every other job passed or was skipped. What gets built ¶ Target Contents Warnings hf_core_deps External driver sources, hf-utils-general, hf-utils-canopen, RtosMutex , BaseThread with its host stub, SignalSemaphore Submodule code: not enforced hf_core Every handler in handlers/ that does not need a specific MCU -Wall -Wextra -Werror hf_core_host_clock FakeClock , the time source for the no-RTOS backend -Wall -Wextra -Werror hf_core_host_mocks Mock* fakes in tests/host/mocks/ -Wall -Wextra -Werror hf_core_host_test_main The HF_TEST / CHECK harness and main() -Wall -Wextra -Werror test_doc_snippets The code shown on this site ( tests/docs/ ), run against the mocks -Wall -Wextra -Werror Handlers left out: WS2812 (needs the ESP32 RMT peripheral), Dynamixel and the CANopenNode slave (both need third-party checkouts that live outside hf-core). Set HF_CORE_ENABLE_<CHIP> before configuring to change the selection. Submodule headers are included as system headers, so warnings inside a driver do not fail hf-core's build. That is deliberate: each submodule is its own repository with its own CI. hf-core's own files are held to the strict flags. Time and threads on the host ¶ With no RTOS there is no tick. By default the no-RTOS backend returns 0 from every clock and returns from every delay at once, so a driver that polls the clock waiting for a timeout would spin forever. The host build defines HF_RTOS_NONE_EXTERNAL_CLOCK , which routes os_time_get() , os_delay_msec() , os_get_elapsed_time_msec() and RtosTime::GetCurrentTimeUs() to hf::host::FakeClock ( tests/host/mocks/FakeClock.h ): a delay advances the clock by the requested time and returns at once; every clock read advances the clock by 10 µs, so polling loops reach their timeout after a bounded number of reads; FakeClock::AdvanceMs() , SetAutoAdvanceUs(0) , TotalDelayUs() and DelayCount() let a test control and check time; the test runner calls FakeClock::Reset() before each case. A 200 ms SH-2 timeout in the BNO08x driver therefore costs microseconds of real time. BaseThread works without a scheduler: StartThreadAndWaitToVerify() runs Setup() inline and marks the thread running, and the test calls Step() itself (applying the returned delay with os_delay_msec() if it matters). RtosMutex and MutexLockGuard lock and unlock but never block. The mocks ¶ Include HfCoreMocks.h and link hf_core_host_mocks . All fakes live in namespace hf::host , record every call, and inject failures on demand. Fake Answers with Inspect / inject MockI2c Queued reads ( QueueRead ), then a responder callback, then an optional register model ( EnableRegisterModel , SetRegister , SetReadOnly ), then zeros Transactions() , WritesTo(reg) , CountOf(kind) , FailNext(err, n) MockSpi Queued MISO frames, then a full-duplex responder, then a fill byte Transactions() (one entry per chip-select frame), FailNext MockGpio Inputs read SetInputLevel() ; outputs read back what was driven LevelHistory() , DrivenLevel() , FireInterrupt() , FailReads/FailWrites MockAdc Per-channel voltage or count, optional queued sequence ReadCount(ch) , FailChannel(ch) MockCan InjectRx() frames go to the receive callback or the RX queue, through the acceptance filter SentFrames() , FailNextSend , SetBusOff MockNvs Typed in-memory store (u32, string, blob) with ESP-IDF key limits CommitCalls() , FailNext , SetReadOnly MockUart InjectRx() bytes; SetOnWrite() answers a request when it is sent TxBytes() , TxWrites() , FailNextWrite MockTemperature SetCelsius() ReadCalls() , Fail() Like real peripherals, the fakes follow Base* lazy initialization: call EnsureInitialized() (handlers do this themselves) before using a fake directly. tests/host/test_mocks.cpp is the executable description of their behaviour. For devices with a protocol, write a small model on top of a responder. The handler tests show three patterns: a register file ( test_pcal95555.cpp ), a pipelined SPI register map with CRC ( test_as5047u.cpp ), and a framed request/response protocol (SHTP in test_bno08x.cpp , TMCL in test_tmc9660.cpp ). From a board HAL ¶ A HAL's host test build adds hf-core as a subdirectory. Its unit tests stay off; the libraries, mocks and harness are built. # HAL host CMakeLists.txt (host builds only) set ( HF_CORE_ENABLE_TMC5160 OFF ) # optional: narrow the handler set add_subdirectory ( lib/core hf-core ) add_executable ( test_fan_manager test_fan_manager.cpp src/FanManager.cpp ) target_link_libraries ( test_fan_manager PRIVATE hf_core_host_mocks hf_core_host_test_main ) add_test ( NAME fan_manager COMMAND test_fan_manager ) A test in the HAL then looks like this one, which hf-core's own host build compiles and runs: tests/docs/host_test.cpp #include "HfCoreMocks.h" #include "HostTest.h" #include "Pcal95555Handler.h" HF_TEST ( Expander_DrivesPinThreeAsOutput ) { hf :: host :: MockI2c i2c ( 0x21 ); // BaseI2c fake at the expander's address i2c . EnableRegisterModel (); // reads return what was written i2c . SetRegister ( 0x06 , 0xFF ); // CONFIG0: all pins inputs at power-on i2c . SetRegister ( 0x07 , 0xFF ); Pcal95555Handler expander ( i2c ); REQUIRE ( expander . EnsureInitialized ()); CHECK ( expander . SetDirection ( 3 , hf_gpio_direction_t :: HF_GPIO_DIRECTION_OUTPUT ) == hf_gpio_err_t :: GPIO_SUCCESS ); CHECK (( i2c . GetRegister ( 0x06 ) & ( 1u << 3 )) == 0 ); // bit 3 cleared: output } Managers that take Base* references, not Esp* or Stm* types, can be tested this way unchanged on any target MCU. The MCU boundary ¶ The host build is the check that code above the MCU layer stays portable: if it compiles and links with HF_CORE_MCU=NONE , it does not depend on a vendor SDK. MCU boundary lists the files that may include one. Next: Examples .

docs.text: Integration ¶ How a project builds hf-core: platform selection, feature switches, the variables the build settings return and how a HAL or an ESP-IDF component consumes them. One file for every consumer ¶ cmake/hf_core_build_settings.cmake is the only build entry point on target. It does not create a target: it fills variables, and the consumer registers them in whatever its build system wants (an ESP-IDF component, a plain CMake library, an STM32 project). Each external driver's own build_settings.cmake stays the source of truth for that driver's files; hf-core includes it when the driver's switch is on. Platform selection ¶ Set both before the include() . Variable Values Default Effect HF_CORE_MCU ESP32 , STM32 , NONE ESP32 Which inc/mcu/<mcu>/ implementations of the Base* interfaces are compiled; NONE compiles none HF_CORE_RTOS FREERTOS , THREADX , NONE FREERTOS Which RTOS sources of hf-utils-rtos-wrap are compiled and whether HF_THREAD_SAFE=1 is defined HF_CORE_CANOPENNODE_ROOT path ${HF_HAL_ROOT}/third_party/CANopenNode Upstream CANopenNode, needed only by HF_CORE_ENABLE_CANOPENNODE The foundation is always compiled for the selected MCU: SPI, I2C, GPIO, ADC, NVS, logger, temperature and periodic-timer implementations, the RTOS wrapper and hf-utils-general. Feature switches ¶ Every driver, handler, optional interface and utility group has a switch. The feature switch reference lists all of them with defaults and the definitions they add. Three rules: Everything is off by default except HF_CORE_ENABLE_LOGGER . A driver turns on what it needs : TMC5160, TMC9660, Alicat BASIS-2, FDO2 and Dynamixel turn on UART; WS2812 turns on RMT; NTC and MCP9700 turn on ADC. A driver tied to one MCU's peripheral fails at configure time on another MCU (WS2812 needs the ESP32 RMT). Outputs ¶ Variable Contents HF_CORE_SOURCES Every .c / .cpp file to compile: interfaces, RTOS, utilities, CANopen, handlers, drivers HF_CORE_INCLUDE_DIRS Include directories for all of them HF_CORE_IDF_REQUIRES ESP-IDF components ( driver , freertos , esp_driver_spi , ...; esp_driver_uart , esp_driver_twai , esp_adc , esp_driver_rmt when needed); empty for other MCUs HF_CORE_COMPILE_DEFINITIONS HF_MCU_FAMILY_<MCU>=1 , HF_RTOS_<RTOS>=1 , HF_THREAD_SAFE=1 with an RTOS, HARDFOC_RTOS_WRAP=1 , HARDFOC_CORE_UTILS=1 , HARDFOC_CORE_DRIVERS=1 and one HARDFOC_<CHIP>_SUPPORT=1 per enabled driver HF_CORE_ROOT The hf-core folder Configuration prints a summary of the enabled features, interfaces and source counts. In an ESP-IDF component ¶ examples/esp32/components/hf_core/CMakeLists.txt is the reference: it enables every handler the examples test, includes the build settings and registers the outputs with idf_component_register() . It also sets the per-target MCU definitions ( HF_TARGET_MCU_ESP32S3=1 and so on) and the WS2812 Kconfig values. In a board HAL ¶ A HAL sets its subset and includes the same file. The Vortex V1 HAL, for example: set ( HF_CORE_MCU "ESP32" ) set ( HF_CORE_RTOS "FREERTOS" ) set ( HF_CORE_ENABLE_TMC9660 ON ) set ( HF_CORE_ENABLE_AS5047U ON ) set ( HF_CORE_ENABLE_BNO08X ON ) set ( HF_CORE_ENABLE_PCAL95555 ON ) set ( HF_CORE_ENABLE_PCA9685 ON ) set ( HF_CORE_ENABLE_NTC_THERMISTOR ON ) set ( HF_CORE_ENABLE_WS2812 ON ) set ( HF_CORE_ENABLE_CAN ON ) set ( HF_CORE_ENABLE_UTILS_CANOPEN ON ) set ( HF_CORE_ENABLE_VORTEX_DRIVER ON ) include ( "${CMAKE_CURRENT_LIST_DIR}/lib/core/cmake/hf_core_build_settings.cmake" ) On the host ¶ The top-level CMakeLists.txt is the host build only (it refuses to cross-compile). It sets HF_CORE_MCU=NONE , HF_CORE_RTOS=NONE , turns on every handler that does not need an MCU peripheral or a third-party checkout, and creates the hf_core , hf_core_host_mocks and hf_core_host_test_main libraries. A HAL's host tests use it with add_subdirectory() . See Host build and mocks . Next: Feature switches .

docs.text: MCU boundary ¶ Which files may include a vendor SDK, how the host build enforces it, and where ESP32, STM32 and CAN FD support stand. The rule ¶ Everything in hf-core above the Base* interfaces is MCU-agnostic. It may include only Base* headers, OsAbstraction.h / OsUtility.h and HandlerCommon.h for platform services. docs.text: Quickstart ¶ Add hf-core to an ESP-IDF project, turn on one handler and drive a chip through it. The example uses the PCA9555 / PCAL9555A I/O expander because it needs only an I2C device. Every handler follows the same steps. Add the repository. hf-core and its submodules (the drivers, the interface wrap, the utilities) go in one checkout: git submodule add https://github.com/hardfoc/hf-core.git lib/core git submodule update --init --recursive lib/core Check it out as a folder named core : sources include core/... paths, which resolve from the folder above it. Any other name works too; the build settings then expose the tree as core/ through a link in the build directory. Choose the handlers. In the CMakeLists.txt of the component that builds hf-core, set the switches you need, include the build settings and register what they collect: components/hf_core/CMakeLists.txt set ( HF_CORE_MCU "ESP32" ) set ( HF_CORE_RTOS "FREERTOS" ) set ( HF_CORE_ENABLE_PCAL95555 ON ) include ( "${CMAKE_CURRENT_LIST_DIR}/../../lib/core/cmake/hf_core_build_settings.cmake" ) idf_component_register ( SRCS ${ HF_CORE_SOURCES } INCLUDE_DIRS ${ HF_CORE_INCLUDE_DIRS } REQUIRES ${ HF_CORE_IDF_REQUIRES } ) set_property ( TARGET ${ COMPONENT_LIB } PROPERTY CXX_STANDARD 20 ) target_compile_definitions ( ${ COMPONENT_LIB } PUBLIC ${ HF_CORE_COMPILE_DEFINITIONS } ) Drive the chip. The handler takes the expander's BaseI2c device, which the board HAL creates (on ESP32, an EspI2cDevice from an EspI2cBus ): tests/docs/quickstart.cpp #include "HandlerCommon.h" #include "Pcal95555Handler.h" // `i2c` is the expander's BaseI2c device, created by the board HAL // (an EspI2cDevice on ESP32, a hf::host::MockI2c in a host test). bool BlinkStatusLed ( BaseI2c & i2c ) { Pcal95555Handler expander ( i2c ); // no bus traffic yet if ( ! expander . EnsureInitialized ()) { // probes the chip once return false ; // wiring, address or power } constexpr uint8_t kLedPin = 3 ; if ( expander . SetDirection ( kLedPin , hf_gpio_direction_t :: HF_GPIO_DIRECTION_OUTPUT ) != hf_gpio_err_t :: GPIO_SUCCESS ) { return false ; } for ( int i = 0 ; i < 6 ; ++ i ) { if ( expander . Toggle ( kLedPin ) != hf_gpio_err_t :: GPIO_SUCCESS ) { return false ; } handler_utils :: DelayMs ( 250 ); } return true ; } What each step does ¶ Step What happens Pcal95555Handler expander(i2c) Stores the reference. No bus traffic, no allocation of the driver yet EnsureInitialized() Creates the driver, probes the chip and caches the port registers; later calls return at once SetDirection() , Toggle() Each locks the handler's mutex, so two tasks can share one handler handler_utils::DelayMs() vTaskDelay on ESP-IDF, the OS abstraction elsewhere, the fake clock in host tests The same function runs unchanged in a host test against hf::host::MockI2c ; the host build does exactly that ( tests/docs/doc_snippets_test.cpp ). If it does not work ¶ Symptom Check CMake: Unsupported MCU HF_CORE_MCU is one of ESP32 , STM32 , NONE CMake: a driver's build_settings.cmake not found The submodules are not initialised: git submodule update --init --recursive Link errors for Esp* classes The interface is optional: set HF_CORE_ENABLE_UART , _CAN , _PWM or _PIO EnsureInitialized() returns false Address straps, pull-ups, power; the bus itself must be initialised by the HAL Driver 'WS2812' requires MCU=ESP32 The WS2812 handler needs the ESP32 RMT peripheral Next: Integration for every switch and output, or the handler catalogue .

docs.text: Threading and RTOS ¶ How hf-core locks, waits and runs tasks without naming an RTOS: the selection, the primitives and what they do on the host. The RTOS is chosen once ¶ HF_CORE_RTOS picks the backend at configure time and defines HF_RTOS_<NAME>=1 . Code above the backends uses OsAbstraction.h / OsUtility.h ( os_delay_msec() , os_time_get() , the OS_* types) and the C++ classes of hf-utils-rtos-wrap , never FreeRTOS headers. HF_CORE_RTOS Backend header HF_THREAD_SAFE Used by FREERTOS os/os_freertos.h 1 ESP-IDF builds, both board HALs THREADX os/os_threadx.h 1 Selectable; no consumer yet NONE os/os_none.h not defined The host build; bare-metal bring-up The rtos wrapper also has a CMSIS-RTOS header ( os/os_cmsis.h , HF_RTOS_CMSIS ); the build settings do not offer it yet. The primitives ¶ Class Header Use it for RtosMutex RtosMutex.h The handler lock: recursive, lock() , try_lock_for(ms) , unlock() MutexLockGuard RtosMutex.h RAII lock on an RtosMutex ( RtosUniqueLock<RtosMutex> ), optional timeout, IsLocked() BaseThread BaseThread.h A task with Setup() , Step() (returns the delay to the next step) and Cleanup() PeriodicTimer PeriodicTimer.h A software timer calling a function OsQueue , OsEventFlags , SignalSemaphore same names Passing items, flags and signals between tasks CriticalGuard CriticalGuard.h A short critical section handler_utils::DelayMs() , DelayUs() handlers/common/HandlerCommon.h Delays inside handlers, on any platform A class guarding its own state: tests/docs/threading.cpp class Counter { public : void Add ( uint32_t n ) noexcept { MutexLockGuard lock ( mutex_ ); // released on every return path total_ += n ; } uint32_t Total () noexcept { MutexLockGuard lock ( mutex_ , 10 ); // wait at most 10 ms return lock . IsLocked () ? total_ : 0 ; } private : RtosMutex mutex_ ; // recursive: a locked method may call another one uint32_t total_ { 0 }; }; A task that owns a sensor read: tests/docs/threading.cpp class FlowTask : public BaseThread { public : explicit FlowTask ( SfmHandler & meter ) noexcept : BaseThread ( "flow" ), meter_ ( meter ) {} protected : bool Initialize () noexcept override { // creates the task on a static stack return CreateBaseThread ( stack_ , sizeof ( stack_ ), 5 , 5 , 0 , OS_AUTO_START ); } bool ResetVariables () noexcept override { samples_ = 0 ; return true ; } bool Setup () noexcept override { return meter_ . EnsureInitialized (); } uint32_t Step () noexcept override { if ( meter_ . ReadMeasurement ()) { ++ samples_ ; } return 100 ; // ms until the next Step() } bool Cleanup () noexcept override { return true ; } private : SfmHandler & meter_ ; uint32_t samples_ { 0 }; uint8_t stack_ [ 4096 ]{}; }; // Start it from the code that owns the handler: // FlowTask task(meter); // task.EnsureInitialized() && task.StartThreadAndWaitToVerify(1000); Mutexes inside the interface wrap ¶ hf-internal-interface-wrap cannot depend on the RTOS wrapper, so its PlatformMutex defaults to a no-op backend. hf-core supplies the real one: handlers/common/PlatformMutexBackend.h is on the include path, and PlatformMutex.h picks it up with __has_include . With HF_RTOS_FREERTOS it maps to a FreeRTOS mutex; with HF_RTOS_NONE it stays a no-op. A standalone build of the interface wrap therefore has no locking. On the host ¶ With HF_RTOS_NONE there is no scheduler and no tick. The host build defines HF_RTOS_NONE_EXTERNAL_CLOCK and routes every clock read and delay to hf::host::FakeClock : a delay advances the clock and returns, and each clock read advances it by 10 µs, so polling loops reach their timeouts. BaseThread runs Setup() inline in StartThreadAndWaitToVerify() and the test calls Step() itself. RtosMutex locks and unlocks but never blocks. Details: Host build and mocks . Next: MCU boundary .

docs.text: Figures ¶ Every figure on this site is drawn by a Python module from facts extracted from the code, so it is rebuilt, not redrawn, when the code changes. CI runs hardfoc-docs figures --check and fails when a committed figure no longer matches the code. Each figure below lists the files it is drawn from. Where hf-core sits ¶ Where hf-core sits Figure description and sources From the bottom up. Each device driver is its own repository and talks to its chip through a small CRTP interface; hf-core-drivers collects them as submodules, together with hf-internal-interface-wrap (the Base* interfaces and their ESP32 and STM32 implementations) and hf-pincfg. hf-core-utils collects the RTOS wrapper, the general utilities and the CANopen helpers. hf-core's handlers sit on top of those three: each one wraps one driver behind a thread-safe API that takes Base* interfaces. A board HAL creates the MCU peripherals, constructs the handlers it needs and exposes managers; a product is firmware on one board HAL. The driver list is read from cmake/hf_core_build_settings.cmake and the handler list from handlers/.
